ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Cardiology Referral — Franklin D. Roosevelt — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Primary care visit for breathlessness, orthopnea, and leg swelling

text.paragraph: Please evaluate and advise on hypertensive heart disease with heart failure and chronic systolic (congestive) heart failure and nicotine dependence, cigarettes, uncomplicated and sequelae of poliomyelitis and prediabetes and hyperlipidemia, unspecified. [S]
Cardiology referral to confirm the diagnosis, review the echocardiogram, and guide titration. [S]
Referral for the concerns below, which began before the index visit. [S]

list.item: Breathlessness, poor sleep from orthopnea, and leg swelling are cutting short his workdays. [S]
Wants to stop smoking without losing his edge at work. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Franklin Delano Roosevelt was born on January 30, 1882, at Springwood, the family's estate in Hyde Park, New York. [D]

In the summer of 1921 Roosevelt developed a paralytic illness at Campobello; on August 25, 1921, Dr. Robert Lovett diagnosed infantile paralysis (polio), and Roosevelt remained paraplegic, using leg braces from early 1922. [D]

A 2003 Bayesian analysis of the recorded symptoms concluded that Guillain-Barré syndrome was more probable than paralytic polio as the cause of Roosevelt's 1921 illness; the conclusion is disputed and cannot be confirmed because no cerebrospinal fluid was examined. [R]
In May 1941 Roosevelt had severe iron deficiency anemia, with hemoglobin reported at 4.5 g/100 mL. [D]

At an examination at Bethesda Naval Hospital on March 27, 1944, Roosevelt's blood pressure was 186/108; he was breathless and cyanotic with rales, and X-rays and an electrocardiogram showed an enlarged heart, congestive heart failure, and a mitral murmur. His blood pressure had not been checked since February 27, 1941. [D]

After the March 1944 examination Roosevelt was treated with digitalis, a low-sodium and weight-reduction diet, and rest; his working hours were reduced, his cigarettes were limited to ten a day, and his evening cocktails were reduced. [D]
Roosevelt's father, James Roosevelt, died in 1900 during Franklin's first term at Harvard; his mother, Sara Delano Roosevelt, died at Springwood in September 1941. [D]

Start guideline-directed therapy for HFrEF: sacubitril/valsartan, carvedilol, and empagliflozin, with furosemide for congestion; add spironolactone after the two-week potassium check. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022) [S]

Check a basic metabolic panel one to two weeks after each renin-angiotensin or mineralocorticoid antagonist change, then every three to six months when stable. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, heart failure and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Treat to a blood pressure below 130/80 with home blood pressure and daily weight logs; low-sodium diet. Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, heart failure and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]

Give intravenous ferric carboxymaltose for iron deficiency with ferritin below 100 ng/mL and transferrin saturation below 20%. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022) [S]
Tobacco cessation counseling with nicotine replacement and a quit date. Guideline: Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

Repeat echocardiogram three to six months after reaching tolerated doses to decide on device therapy. Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, heart failure and hypertension monographs (2026) [S]
